[b]The Sealiph of Irocco, Bearer of the Seal of Interpretation

To His Excellency, Fereydun Khan, President of the Republic of Dhornaper

In the Name of Allah, the Compassionate, the Merciful[/b]

The Sealiphate of Irocco finds the proposal acceptable, and that due reverence has been paid to our station, though our might has waned over recent years. I, Ibrahim, will attend this summit myself. Such Pan-Shamatine matters of vital continental economic sovereignty are not to be devoluted to my subordinates. While I am present in your resplendent state, would it be possible to enter into formal diplomatic relations? Of course, this may be discussed at a later date between diplomats, but when two great men can meet and talk for their nations, then why deny us such an opportunity? Either way, I hope for the success of this summit.

Peace be upon those who follow the guidance,

Bearer of the Seal of Interpretation,
Sealiph,

Ibrahim ibn Gakh'ud Al Iyaiid

[i][u][b]Pre History[/b][/u]

Irakqaist was under the rule of the Shah Al-Shiv Dynasty for centuries. However, when King Shah Munkial Al-Shiv decided to bring modernization through the adoption of Western ideas of a secular society, things began to change. In early 1956, he introduced revolutionary ideas by prohibiting hijabs for females and by compelling Muslims to burn the Qur'an. However, this angered many people and landed the throne of the kingdom under threat. To suppress the rebellion, King Munkial used his secret police force and arrested and executed those who opposed his ideas.

Amidst the fear, a resistance began to emerge. On June 16, 1957, the Islamic League of Isa'ath Revolutionaries was formed as a militant movement organization. The new ideology of Isaathism sought to unify the nation under Sharia law while incorporating aspects of Baathist throughout its movemnt. Isaathism rejected liberalism, secularism, Western influence, and corruption, yet it embraced nationalism and multicultural coexistence, allowing freedom of religion and respect for all citizens of Irakqaist. It promoted the belief that social and political governance should follow the Quran and Baathist principles, while economic policy and foreign relations could operate under a regulated free market guided by the Isaath state. The overarching goal of Isaathism was to unite the Ummah, bring peace and stability to the kingdom, and establish justice for all.

The Isaath networks continued their agenda through the means of education and mosques, as well as the use of hidden caves to communicate their plans in an unnoticeable manner to the state. Between 1957 and 1968, known as The Reform of Blood, witnessed Munkial Al-Shiv attempting to industrialize the kingdom and hold absolute power through monopolized elites and laissez-faire policies. Contrary to expecting stability, these measures further divided and incited violence in the kingdom. The Isaath Message networks disseminated their ideologies via secretive means in schools, mosques, and deep cave networks, opting to keep a low profile as the kingdom maintained oppressive violence. Terrorist strikes became almost commonplace, with the most notorious being the Alka Attack on May 12, 1966, when the Hajkia Jihab militants stormed a government administrative center, killing fifty people and wounding 158, demonstrating the instability of the reign of the Shah. 

The end of the Shah came as a surprise on July 19, 1968. Munkial Al-Shiv, who had been intoxicated following the hosting of an elite party, was assassinated by his own driver, Monhand Herisn. Two weeks later, Herisn was found in his apartment, where he had intended to execute a suicide bombing. The police had to act, killing him in the process, which left twenty-three people dead and fifteen injured. The assassination signaled the end of the violent rule of Munkial.

Shah Karmall III inherited the throne in 1969 following the violent and tumultuous death of his brother, Munkial Al-Shiv. Though the reign of Munkial had been extremely violent and repressive, Shah Karmall IIIs reign had been even more tyrannical and erratic. His Industrialization and adoption of the Western ideals of liberalization had been more tyrannical and violent, taking away more rights from the minorities belonging to the religious and ethnic groups, and his excesses had alienated him from his people as well as the aristocracy.

The reign of terror provoked by Karmall III was so great that loyal military personnel and administrators began plotting against him. One of these plotters was General Farid al-Nashir, a senior officer in King Karmall IIIs royal guard, who was sympathetic to Isaath. Another was Rami Qudrat, frustrated Minister of Finance, secretly allocating funding to Isaath-supported networks, who plotted against King Karmall III to bring an end to his destructive regime.

In 1975, the plotters struck. Forces loyal to the Shah were thus eliminated by bribery, intimidation, and well-coordinated surprise attacks. The palace was encircled, and communication was severed to avoid any call for external or loyalist troops to be sent to succor the palace. However, when Karmall III got the full extent of the deception, he tried to muster his remaining troops, although it was all too little, too late, since most of his loyal followers had already switched sides to join the plotters. In the face of utter isolation and capture, Karmall III was left with no choice but to abdicate the throne in favor of a provisional council led by Isaath supporters.
[/i]
